analysis.title: Something Is Rotten In The State of Yields
key_insights: Treasury, European sovereign and credit markets all showed unusual price action on Thursday. The author argues the root cause of higher Treasury yields is a global supply glut of sovereign and corporate debt, not economic variables, inflation or Fed independence.

Corporate issuance has pulled duration out of the market because companies needing longer-dated bonds have dominated flow. The author cites back-to-back record high-yield deals and a $10 billion corporate deal that is now routine.

The author says there is no shortage of bearish reasons for Treasuries: oil and diesel prices, the deficit, debt trajectory, interest payments above discretionary spending, global and corporate supply, and Saudi Arabia moving from Treasury buyer to needing a loan.
Positioning does not match the bearish narrative. Most commentary seen by the author was bullish or neutral, and the author's own T-Report was neutral on Treasuries going into the week.

The proposed mechanism for the 10-year move from 4.6% on August 25 to 5.27% on Friday is selling driven by low-conviction long positions, thin real liquidity in electronic markets, and systematic momentum and stop-triggering algos that add to shorts as yields rise.

Once selling stops producing more selling, the systematic shorts would be cut quickly and the author expects a sharp snap higher in price and lower in yields. Oil and diesel are the issues most likely to fix themselves and end the cycle.
TLT has received large inflows and its shares outstanding are at the highest level since late 2024, which the author reads as consistent with there being no real bears.

French and Italian yields rose sharply relative to German yields. The French deficit is heading to about 5% against the EU 3% target. The author finds German yields acting as a safe haven odd given its industrial decline and political shift.

The author reads the move as possible unwinds of positions that treated France and Italy as the same risk as Germany, and as a possible sign of markets questioning EU integration. The author calls it a crack, not a canyon, and is not in alarm mode.

Credit: PSKY 8.875% second-lien bonds due 2034 (BB composite), issued at par on a $4 billion deal, traded below 95% on Thursday and 96% on Friday, closing the week at 96.5%, a loss of about $140 million.
HYG, JNK, LQD and VCSH were all trading at NAV, which the author reads as orderly liquidity and the reason credit does not make them nervous yet.
CDX widened from 50 to 60 in two weeks while the Bloomberg Corp OAS moved from 75 bps to 82 bps. CDX was wider Thursday and flat Friday while the S&P 500 rose, a decoupling the author flags.
VIX is barely above 15 against a yearly average of 18. MOVE is 107, just below its March peak of 115 and well above its 1-year average of 74.

The author starts the week neutral on rates after fading the Friday move, but is nervous about European sovereigns and is paying serious attention to credit spreads. The author thinks equities are ignoring fixed income signals.

macro_indicators.reading: 5.27% Friday close, 5.15% low at 8:31am ET Friday, 4.6% on August 25
macro_indicators.interpretation: The yield rose about 67 bps in roughly five weeks, and the speed of the move concerns the author as much as the level.
Just below the March peak of 115 and well above the 1-year average of 74, so bond volatility is elevated.
Well below the yearly average of 18, so equity volatility is low relative to bond volatility.
Widened from 50 over two weeks, below the almost 70 reached in March at the start of the war.
Up from 75 bps, a smaller move than CDX.
Helps explain the rise in French and Italian yields relative to German yields.

trade_ideas.description: Fade the Treasury rally on Friday morning after the jobs data
trade_ideas.rationale: The author expected the post-data rally in Treasuries to fade by the end of the day. The 10-year moved from 5.15% to 5.27%.

risk_factors: Selling in Treasuries may keep begetting selling until bulls show conviction or positioning turns bearish.
Further unwinds in European sovereign relative-value positions would make borrowing harder for Italy and France.
Renewed market questioning of EU economic integration.
Credit spreads, CDX in particular, could be an early sign of broader stress, and the author flags the decoupling from equities.
Equities may be ignoring fixed income signals.
Oil and diesel prices remain a bond market headwind.
vol_and_positioning: MOVE index at 107, below the March peak of 115 and above the 1-year average of 74.
VIX barely above 15 versus a yearly average of 18.
TLT shares outstanding are at the highest level since late 2024 after large inflows.
Positioning in Treasuries is described as many small low-conviction longs, with systematic momentum and stop-hunting algos driving selling that begets more selling.
HYG, JNK, LQD and VCSH trade at NAV, so there is no ETF discount signal of dislocation.
CDX decoupled from the S&P 500 on Thursday and Friday.
geopolitical: A possible deal with Iran is named as a potential help to markets.
Higher oil and diesel prices are cited as a bearish factor for Treasuries, and Europe's release of diesel from its strategic reserve is attributed to Macron.
CDX peaked near 70 in March at the start of the war.
Saudi Arabia has gone from a Treasury buyer to needing a loan to fund operations.
The author raises EU cohesion questions, including Frexit-style risk and countries acting in their own national interest.

tension_points.bull_case: Positioning is mostly long or neutral with low conviction, TLT inflows are large, and when selling stops feeding itself the systematic shorts will cut and yields snap lower.
tension_points.bear_case: Global sovereign and corporate supply, oil and diesel, deficits and interest costs support higher yields, and selling begets selling in a momentum-driven market.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Selling no longer producing more selling, or oil and diesel prices resolving, would end the cycle and trigger a snap lower in yields.

tension_points.bull_case: HYG, JNK, LQD and VCSH trade at NAV, indicating orderly liquidity, and CDX at 60 is below March's near 70.
tension_points.bear_case: CDX widened from 50 to 60 in two weeks and decoupled from the S&P 500, and the PSKY deal traded below par after a record high-yield issue.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Credit ETFs trading at a discount to NAV would signal dislocation and the ETF death spiral.

theme_stances.key_argument: Low-conviction long positioning and systematic momentum selling push yields higher, and supply, not fundamentals, is the root cause.
French and Italian yields rising relative to German yields is an odd repricing of relative credit risk that may signal a deeper problem.
theme_stances.evidence: I don’t know what is going on here, but it does not seem good.
